speechtext:
motion No. 12 as follows:
That Bill C-201, an act to provide for the review and assessment of acquisitions of control of Canadian business enterprises by certain persons, be amended by deleting line 25 on page 12 thereof and substituting therefor the following:
"based on such information and evidence; and, where the opinion is that the person is not a non-eligible person, the minister and his successors in office shall, upon such information and evidence, be bound by that opinion."
He said: Mr. Speaker, the reason I have put forward this amendment is that it embodies the point of view put forward by certain committee members including myself, as well as many of the witnesses who wished to simplify the administration of this legislation by eliminating as much as possible the necessity of having to come to the minister for every transaction. Every transaction which might be considered to be caught by the act would have to be brought to the minister. That would include everyone who is close to the limits but who has established that for the purposes of this act the control is Canadian. Having done that once, surely it is possible for that person or corporation to look forward to a period of peace during which he would not, every time in respect of every transaction, have to come to the minister. If the minister has granted a certificate there should for a time be some reliance placed upon that certificate.
I would place this matter where the onus should lie, that is, with the minister and not with the corporation. Why should the companies always bear the onus of establishing their innocence? It seems to me fundamental that companies should have the presumption in their favour. If having obtained a certificate from information which may be obtained by the minister or lodged with him there is some doubt as to the company's status, the certificate, having been granted some time before, could be called into question. But the onus would be on the ministry: that is where it should be.
This is not the Income Tax Act, although the minister in all cases has acted in the spirit of the Income Tax Act. In other words, the Canadian citizen, the Canadian corporation, must establish its innocence. Since when is that a generally acceptable principle of law or of conduct? We hear everywhere, all along the line, that the individual is the person under this legislation who must establish that there is significant benefit to Canada. The onus is wrong. The government is establishing the regulatory agency; let it act. Why should the responsibility be that of the individual? It is all too easy for government to act in that way. I for one find this provision totally repugnant. It is a matter of personal repugnance to me that in dealing with government it is always the individual who must prove his innocence. That to my mind is not part of a democratic society.
This is the spirit of the amendment. The administration could be handled much easier on the basis of my proposal. If the minister in accepting the principle that I have

put forward should have an alternative formula, I am quite open in this regard. I recognize there is no solution that would be 100 per cent in respect of acceptance of my point of view. Perhaps a certificate that is good for three years on balance would be the best method. Once a certificate were granted and the company had not materially changed its circumstances, the certificate would be valid for three years unless revoked. On the other hand, the certificate could be granted for an indefinite period subject to revocation. These are two avenues of approach. But it seems to me it would be infinitely more acceptable, infinitely more just and infinitely less costly, with much less red tape involved, than the procedure now required by the minister where the responsibility lies with the individual person as determined by this legislation.
It must be remembered that every time the government introduces legislation of this kind, the cost in time and endeavour by the citizen or the businessman is an additional cost. The good Lord only knows how in the past quarter of a century costs which are really the responsibility of the government have been piled on the backs of business and economic activity throughout the country. Who pays for the cost of compiling and maintaining unemployment insurance records and filings on behalf of employees? Who pays for the cost of collection of income tax at source? It is the employer. Who pays for the compilation of the Canada Pension Plan and the computation thereof? The employer. Who pays for health insurance, medicare and so on? Then we have Statistics Canada which comes along with a whole series of requests for information so that a business which employs 25 or 30 persons must hire one or two more merely to maintain records for the government. I did forget that there are also workmen's compensation levies and reports. That item is also a cost that is loaded on the back of the employer.
Who pays for these things in the end? It is the consumer, the Canadian public. All these requirements are fed into the machine. Bureaucracy piles upon bureaucracy, increasing the price which has to be paid by the ultimate consumer, John Citizen. What benefit does he get from it? A great deal of it is highly doubtful. This is another instance of the government feeding the cost of more bureaucracy into the economic machine of this country.
It is a completely new departure; it is a completely new input of bureaucracy into the economic affairs of the country. This has to be paid for. I find it repugnant that this should be so. I say it would be far better for the minister to accept proposals which seek to eliminate as much red tape as possible and make it as easy as possible for those involved or coming under the purported jurisdiction of this legislation to carry on their affairs with a minimum of interference, albeit meeting the requirements of the minister under the act. It is for this reason I have put forward this amendment and seek the support of the House for it.

They may be costly but not, certainly, in the way the hon. member attempted to suggest. There is no way I could support this amendment because really what the hon. member for Edmonton West is asking us to do, in the fine moral fury of presumed innocence which he has worked up, is to proceed on the assumption that once somebody receives a clean bill of health so far as ownership is concerned, he should be left alone. It is like saying the lady of the evening has her certificate and therefore one should never look at her again because she is all right.
The hon. member for Edmonton West, who is very knowledgeable about business and the stock market, knows that a certificate could be issued in the morning and in the afternoon the entire ownership of the corporation could be changed. How does one go about saying that once the minister has made a decision, that decision is forever? I realize the difficulty of the situation as suggested by the hon. member, that the onus of proof should be on the government. This is fine. He brings in other cases where this is done. However, in bringing them in the hon. member neglected to indicate that in these cases there is a disclosure mechanism which makes it possible for the onus to lie with the government. For instance, in the case of income tax a person must declare his income annually. The government can review the income tax return and make a decision.
What makes this more surprising, and certainly not understandable so far as the hon. member for Edmonton West is concerned, is that over the years when in this House and in committee we have debated various pieces of legislation, the hon. member has constantly refused to put disclosure regulations in the Corporations Act and other acts.
I do not like the onus being put on the individual or on the corporation. I think this is not a good principle. But unless you have disclosure in the rest of the legislation, which the hon. member for Edmonton West opposes, there is no other choice. If the disclosure were there, the minister could act on the information which came under other acts and we could say to the minister that he has to initiate proceedings in such a case.
The Canada Corporations Act is useless in terms of disclosure; there is no disclosure below the level of $5 million of assets, whereas this bill calls for examination at the level of $250,000. Therefore, the other acts do not enable the minister to have any idea of what is happening. We have run into similar problems with the minister in other areas and we have not yet solved the problem of disclosure. The one thing on which I can agree with the hon. member for Edmonton West is that as a principle the onus should be on the government. But then you have to say in justice that our disclosure legislation must be improved; at least information must be available to us.
Foreign Takeovers Review Act
Recently we had the problem of American corporations in Canada which had made application under the DISC program in the United States. No one was as surprised in Canada as the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) who thought he had received assurances from these good friends of his that they were not going to apply for DISC. He woke up one morning and to his horror found he had been shafted in so many places that he looked like a pincushion. His friends had let him down. He had no way of knowing that they had made this application until some outside, extraneous information came to his attention. This would be the same case.
I cannot see how you can possibly have any kind of meaning in an act as meagre as this one. The inclusion of this amendment would wipe out the entire significance of the provisions, because all you have to do if you are an American corporation is obtain Canadian corporate ownership; you would then be as pure as the driven snow. The minute you obtained your certificate you could do as you pleased and the minister would have to play cops and robbers and chase you all over the country to find out what had taken place. If we tried to get disclosure incorporated into the legislation, then my friends to the right, the Conservative party, would say that this is useless information and that we do not need it, that it is just probing and prying. Obviously we do need it. If this amendment has any significance at all, it is that there must be disclosure.
Again, this bill would have very little meaning because there is no disclosure and because built into the situation the minister already has enough problems in trying to ascertain the disposition of a business or what its shares may be, without adding this provision. So I think that on reflection, if the hon. member for Edmonton West thinks of the problems that would be created by accepting his amendment and if he is really serious about strengthening or improving the bill, he will withdraw his motion.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO CONTROL FOREIGN TAKEOVERS OF CANADIAN COMPANIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this amendment, which I must admit from the jurisdictional relationship point of view does adduce a certain complication, does allow me to indicate one more area where this act is an expression of unilaterally assumed jurisdiction by the Parliament of Canada. The Canadian Bar Association has recommended to the minister that this bill be tested by or referred to the Supreme Court to see whether the government has jurisdiction to deal with a company incorporated under the laws of a province with objects that are limited to activities within that province.
This amendment was designed to authorize an exception to be made by a province, bearing in mind the legitimate interests of provinces in economic activity within their borders. This is something which is not the sole

prerogative of the federal government, extending the unilateral action it has taken, completely disregarding prior consultation with the provinces. The whole question of foreign ownership and of takeovers, so far as the provinces are concerned, was considered in a vacuum; they were not consulted.
I think the minister will agree with me that the provinces have a legitimate interest in the economic activities of companies or businesses that operate within their territorial jurisdictions. This is the first time the government of Canada has dared move into this particular field, which I describe as a form of economic czardom or overseeing.
Therefore I have taken the limited means available to me by proposing that power be given to a provincial government to say to the federal government in this regard, "Keep your cotton-picking hands off." That is a term that has been used by provincial ministers to federal ministers on innumerable occasions. It has been used in dominion-provincial conferences, and that is what is meant by this amendment. There is reason for it. If the minister were on this side of the chamber and looking at the bill, he too would recognize that a province has a legitimate interest in doing this. He could readily see from "le chateau fort du centre du Canada" that an Olympian decision is being delivered with regard to something that is happening strictly within provincial jurisdiction.
This is something that has never come within the control of the government of Canada. The government of Canada has no control whatsoever over a foreign company coming into a province and registering under its laws. It has not one iota of control in law or otherwise. A company may carry on business within provincial jurisdiction, report to the provincial authorities, be held responsible to the courts of the province and have subsidiaries within a province. But now for some reason or other the government of Canada can say, "We will step in if you dare buy the total assets of a public company, or 20 per cent of the shares of a private company operating within the province." I say that that is totally ill-founded in law. It is for that reason that I have put forward this amendment, to highlight again the action I think should have been taken by the government in arriving at the presentation of a law that at least had the agreement of the provinces.
The provinces also have some concern about takeovers and foreign ownership. Is this action to be taken only by the government of Canada? After all, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said, "This is what we are going to do. If some of the provinces are not satisfied with the way in which we are dealing with the question of foreign ownership, let them take their own action." A province which may not be satisfied with the way the federal government is dealing with takeovers or foreign ownership may well say, "We are going to exempt all companies in our province." That would be quite in accord with what the Prime Minister said.
Indeed, the provinces might take stronger action than the federal government has proposed. Some of the provinces have already moved in an ad hoc way. The province of Ontario has moved in a certain direction because it wants more processing of basic resources undertaken in
July 5, 1972

the province; but it has not done much to encourage such processing. Aiter all, it is the buyer who determines in what form he will take the commodity he wants. There is no such thing as monopoly of supply; there are many alternative sources of supply.
The province of Alberta has moved in a certain direction and has imposed further conditions with regard to the development of the tar sands. Extension of a permit was made conditional upon certain Canadianization features. I believe some of the results may be more apparent than real because Canadian resources may not be able to fulfil all the requirements, but at least this was a legitimate step taken by a province with regard to resources within its own jurisdiction, applicable to a company within its jurisdiction.
The government of Canada hasn't a word to say about the operations of Syncrude until it starts to transport oil across the boundary of the province of Alberta into another province or applies to transport oil out of the country. The federal government has no control whatsoever over the output of oil from that development when completed except when it may be transported outside the province, when the pipeline will come under the control of the government of Canada. The transportation, the utilization and the pricing of the oil are not subject to determination by the National Energy Board. The National Energy Board may determine the market area in a certain part of the country but beyond that there is nothing that would apply.
I find it extraordinary that there has been this attempt at unilateral action. It will be very interesting to see the reaction the first time-this is presupposing that the law comes into force-the minister goes contrary to the desires of one of the provinces in regard to something that is entirely within provincial jurisdiction. Notwithstanding the amendment to clause 2(2), if the action should be contrary to the expressed desires of the provinces I would judge that the law would immediately be tested in the Supreme Court of Canada. While this is taking place we will see if the government carries on under the law.
It is with that purpose in mind and to highlight these difficulties that I have brought forth this amendment. As I have said, I do not think the House will support it because I know the attitude of the minister and his advisers. They have shut not one eye but both eyes to the question of jurisdictional competence; but it is a fact of life, Mr. Speaker.
I know it would be a lot easier for the minister if he could move at will through all the corporations of the country. It would be a lot easier administratively, but we are not a unitary state and it is not the Parliament of Canada nor the corporations branch which gives the right of existence to corporations. All that they do comes under the jurisdiction of the provinces, but it seems that the federal government of Canada now says that it will oversee these activities to the extent that it will seek to determine the quality and quantity of ownership.
I hope that all hon. members will recognize the problem and the Frankenstein they will have created if they support the minister in this bill.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it has been obvious to me for some time from the amendments moved by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) and his colleagues and the speeches they have made that far from strengthening this bill they have consistently moved amendments which would weaken an already weak bill. I will come to that in a moment, Mr. Speaker. I do not have much faith in the bill, nor do I have much faith in the desire of this government or this minister to administer the bill in such a way that takeovers which have been going on at a very rapid rate will be stopped. I can think of no way in which the hands of the minister could be tied even more than they are by this weak bill than to approve the amendment moved by the hon. member for Edmonton West.
I say this more in a spirit of regret than in criticism, but Canada has a sorry record going back more than 20 years in the field of economic development in various provinces. Which provinces become involved in actively promoting economic development which does not come from the ordinary forces of market activity and the desire of industry to make profits? Not the province of Ontario, which is very active; not the province of British Columbia; not the province of Alberta where the hon. member for Edmonton West comes from. They are the have-not provinces, those where for various reasons such as small population or distance from markets economic growth has not progressed at a rapid enough rate and large numbers of people are unemployed. They are provinces such as Newfoundland, Nova Scotia and my own province of Manitoba. These are the provinces in which provincial governments through one agency or another have become involved in inducing, enticing and persuading private investors to come and build up industry or use the potential resources.
How have they done this, Mr. Speaker? To a large extent it has been through a kind of competition amongst themselves to see how much they could give the private interests in order to get them to come to their province. The record is a sorry one of failure after failure, disaster after disaster and giveaway after giveaway. Let me briefly give some illustrations of this in case the hon. member for Edmonton West does not know about them. Some years ago the government of Newfoundland was involved in this kind of promotion. Three cases come to mind. There was the tremendous hydroelectric development at Churchill Falls in Labrador which cost several billion dollars and produced a tremendous amount of power. Very little of this is needed in Newfoundland or Labrador, so the bulk of the power will be used in the province of Quebec and the remainder sold as surplus power to New York States.
Within the last week or so the minister of finance in the Conservative government of Newfoundland stated that the deal made by the former government with Brinco was so bad from the point of view of the province that it would

The promoters will do very well and will make money, the province of Quebec will get power at a reasonable rate and the State of New York will get power at a good price, but th epeople of Newfoundland will be the losers on this Brinco deal.
Similarly, tens of millions of dollars have gone into a linerboard plant in Newfoundland. Again, the financial arrangements made between the then Liberal government of Newfoundland and the interests putting up that plant were so bad from the point of view of the people of Newfoundland that the present government has exercised its right to take over the plant. The latest example is the oil refinery at Come-By-Chance on which the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) has served notice that it must comply with the federal government's pollution control standards. Unless within the next three weeks they are prepared to invest another $5 million in improving pollution control equipment at that plant, he will order a shut down of the work.
Or you can consider the proposal of the province of Nova Scotia, made by the former Conservative government, for building a heavy water plant on Cape Breton Island. That plant has been in the process of construction for five years or more and has cost the people of Nova Scotia and the federal government, which is involved in the financing of that plan and in the financing of most plans proposed by the provinces, more than $100 million. That is how much the plant has cost the government of Nova Scotia and the federal government. It is estimated that we shall spend $200 million before-or should I say "if"-that plant produces one pound of heavy water.
Or you may consider something that happened in my province. The former Conservative government entered into an agreement with a mysterious group of financiers in Switzerland who were to build a pulp and paper complex at The Pas in northern Manitoba. As an inducement for coming to Manitoba they were given rights to cut timber in virtually a quarter of the province. About $100 million has been spent on building that plant. Without question there was much overexpenditure and unnecessary spending. Mr. Speaker, 90 per cent or more of that money was put up by the province of Manitoba. So bad did the situation become and so behind were the supposed owners in meeting bills of contractors and workers that they were forced into bankruptcy. The provincial government had to take over that plant. Again, the federal government was involved because under our program of grants to slow growth areas the federal government was obligated to pay substantial amounts of money for that project.
I could go on and on, Mr. Speaker. I am trying to tell the hon. member for Edmonton West that the record of provincial governments of whatever political stripe is bad, not because they are incompetent, not because they cannot do a good job but for other reasons. Provincial Crown corporations and provincial hydroelectric systems, most of which are publicly owned in the provinces, have demonstrated repeatedly that they can operate efficiently and provide service to the people at low cost.

Which provinces encountered difficulties? It was precisely those provinces which were in the worst shape. They suffered from the highest rates of unemployment in this country and were forced by pressure, by the need to do things for their people, into poor deals and poor financial arrangements. Despite that, the hon. member for Edmonton West would move an amendment to this bill which would give the very provinces which have demonstrated repeatedly their inability to execute plans which would benefit their people the power of the veto. In other words, they would have power to veto even the limited proposals which would be made by this government.
It seems to me the hon. member for Edmonton West is saying that the provinces will accept almost any deal which will provide some employment and some economic development; they will accept any deal regardless of cost and the concessions they must give. The hon. member would give them power to veto even the very limited steps which the government will be empowered to take under this bill. That means, although the hon. member for Edmonton West does not say so, that the have-not provinces in the vast majority of cases could say, when the federal government deemed a takeover not to be in the interest of the country as a whole, "We need this takeover and therefore we insist that you do not prevent it." If the hon. member for Edmonton West is so obviously opposed to this bill, instead of moving amendments which would cripple the bill he ought to vote against it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the course of this debate we have supported amendments that would increase the degree of consultation between federal and provincial governments. We felt that this was highly desirable because we think that in making their decisions the two levels of government ought to enjoy a closer relationship. We were agreeable to the amendment suggested by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) which would achieve that end. What we have never wanted-and our position was set out clearly by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow-is a veto power in the hands of the provinces, a power they could exercise against the federal government.
The amendment we are considering supports a kind of economic separatism for it advocates a doctrine that would be totally unacceptable at the constitutional level. I wonder what the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) would say about the constitutional validity of a power which gave each province the right to veto every legislative decision taken by the federal government. I do not think he would approve. He is a concerned member and knows what the effect of such veto would be. At the same time, however, he is prepared to move an amendment that would give the provinces power to veto certain economic-based decisions made in other fields. For some reason or other he distinguishes between economic and political and social activity. That distinction I find hard to make.
If we examine some of the possibilities that might arise, we will see they are pretty horrible to contemplate. I am talking about possibilities that might arise if we gave the provinces the veto power that the amendment would permit. Allegedly, the veto power is justified by the contention that what goes on inside the province and what
July 5, 1972

happens to companies incorporated and operating within provincial boundaries affects only that province and is the sole responsibility, therefore, of the elected representatives of the province. We know that is not true. What happens in one province very much affects the lives of people in other provinces, just as what happens in Canada affects people of other countries and what happens in other countries may affect us all. Therefore, the justification for the veto on the basis of self-determination, on the basis that "It is our own skins that are affected", falls flat.
Consider, for instance, the case of a provincial hydroelectric utility. The electricity sometimes is distributed between provinces; in other cases it is transmitted from a province to a foreign country. Say, for instance, that a province in financial difficulty was made a good offer for its utility, an offer so good that it could not possibly turn it down. Say that it wanted to sell out to a foreign company or concern. If the province could make a reasonably advantageous deal but did not think that provinces ought to assume the kind of responsibilities that we think they should assume, should it be permitted to sell? In other words, should it be given the kind of veto proposed in the amendment?

Only to a limited extent. Actually, we have decided that certain things are important. Really, what the hon. member says, and I think I can say this with justice, is that considerations of foreign ownership are not important to the national interest. The implication is that they should not be considered in the same context as telecommunications, transportation, broadcasting and banking and that each province should in effect be able to make its own law. If you give them veto power, you nullify the whole purpose of a national policy on foreign ownership.
Would the hon. member disagree that we have a constitution which gives this kind of veto power to the provinces in other areas affecting the political structure of Canada? In the field of economics, he is quite prepared to say, "Let the devil take the hindmost and let each province determine its own future and priorities. There is always some validity for this."

Obviously, we want to see each province given as much freedom as possible to determine the thrust of its future. But in the final analysis, on a question like foreign ownership and takeovers in particular the national interest has to be considered. Only the federal government can do that. If an amendment of this kind is accepted there would be a very obvious veto in respect of all decisions made by the federal government. If a province chooses to exercise that veto, the effect would be to nullify any meagre effects this bill might have.

speechtext:
motion No. 14 as follows:
That Bill C-201, an act to provide for the review and assessment of acquisitions of control of Canadian business enterprises by certain persons, be amended by deleting therefrom paragraph (c) of subsection (1) of clause 4.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief. There is in the bill provision for the monitoring of takeovers of companies having a minimum of $250,000 in gross assets and $3 million in gross revenue. The purpose of this amendment is to, in effect, reduce that minimum to zero so that any foreign takeover will come within the purview of the act. The reasons for it might seem rather picayune but they are twofold. Under the present arrangement there are a number of loopholes. I shall give a brief illustration.
It is possible that a foreign corporation interested in gaining a major presence in a certain segment of Canadian economic activity could, rather than undertaking to purchase a Canadian company having in excess of $250,000 in gross assets, purchase a number of Canadian companies having less gross assets and less gross revenue than is provided for in the act. Through small takeovers it could, gradually establish a rather imposing presence within a given area of the economy. That is a prospect which the legislation overlooks, and it is cause for just as much concern potentially as the kind of takeovers which
[Mr. Pepin.)
the government contemplates screening under this legislation.
The other concern which prompted me to submit my amendment is that when initially developed, a good deal of technology is financed on a very marginal basis. It is quite possible that we could lose a good deal, or at least some new technology to foreign corporations in its inception simply because the gross assets involved in the development of technology and the revenue being gained do not meet the limits proposed in the legislation in the early stages of the development. This has been the case with many great technological breakthroughs.
There is also a tendency in Canadian banking institutions to be reluctant to fund Canadian ventures into new areas of technology. This is because they are considered high risk. On the other hand, funding is readily available if a Canadian inventor of some new technology has the potential support of a United States or international corporation for his product. This gives banks the assurance they need before making development capital available.
This is one of the problems of industrial development in Canada, and as written I think the bill does nothing to remedy the situation. It lets the present position prevail whereby new technological development in Canada, owing to the exigencies of the financial world, are quite often unnecessarily thrown into the hands of foreign corporations.
These are the two major reasons for my submitting this amendment and I should like to hear the comments of other hon. members with respect thereto.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the many discussions on foreign ownership one of the matters often debated is whether the future of Canada's industrial development really hinges on buying back these large, monolithic, developed companies which are so set in their ways, which mass produce certain consumer or technical goods, or rather whether the future of this country depends upon finding new areas of development and on putting emphasis on financing such resources.
The hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Rowland) who moved this motion made an excellent point when he said that many new ideas originate in the minds of the staff of small companies. It is here where the most dangerous form of takeover takes place, and the provisions of this bill do nothing to rectify the situation. The reason I say this is the most dangerous form of takeover is that these ideas will generate development in the future.
I can recite a long catalogue of inventions which were conceived in someone's basement or small laboratory and which later formed the basis for the establishment of large corporations. It is not the mature companies that are at the heart of the foreign ownership problem; rather, it is the companies that have their eye on future development. The mature companies are more in the past and if we concentrate on them the future will evade us and foreign ownership will continue ad infinitum.
There are many new technologies developed by mature companies and to this extent we must take an interest in large corporations. But it would be a terrible mistake and
July 5, 1972

a gross oversight to neglect smaller companies in the way the bill does. What possible justification can the drafters of the bill have for the exclusion of small companies? Do they feel that there are so many small companies, that there are so many transfers of businesses, that the situation would be far too complex to deal with? Even if that were the case, would it still not be worth while to look at the situation?
The government would not have to take months and months to scrutinize such takeovers. Most of them would be routine. After all, the corner grocery is not going to be taken over by a large international corporation. The transfer of a small plant is usually from one Canadian to another Canadian, often from one partner to another partner or from one group of stockholders to another group of stockholders.
Small companies that develop unique products often do so with the help of government programs sponsored by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. The department has done worth-while work in terms of assisting inventors in this country to develop new products. Most of these new products are developed by relatively small firms. I presume the reason the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce offers such assistance is not to make a small outlet ripe for takeover by an international corporation but to develop products that are indigenous to this country, and to promote entrepreneural activity.
Unless smaller companies are included within a foreign ownership policy, a great deal of damage will be done. From the administrative point of view it is possible to establish an initial review procedure to approve transfers between Canadians quickly. There is no reason this cannot be done. If because the procedure is quick the odd mistake is made, then this is the price we will have to pay.
I think this review procedure would also provide an enormous opportunity for the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. I have seen many small companies taken over by foreign corporations. After all, no one is going to go after the Steel Company of Canada; it is the small companies that are picked up, the companies that have difficulty getting sufficient financing. This is the sort of company the international corporations look for. Sometimes they are trying to buy out a competing product that might challenge their own. Sometimes they are just gambling, buying up all the new ideas they can. They know that though some will not work, others will. The international corporation loves to do this sort of thing and will continue to do so in view of the exclusion that is built into this bill.
Let me return to what I said earlier about the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce having an enormous opportunity here. If the clause setting the limit at $250,000 were removed and all takeovers had to be scrutinized, the minister's department would have a golden opportunity. For example, if they asked a company why it wanted to sell out to a foreigner and the company replied that it had not been able to get any financing, the departmental officials would then know that the company was having problems and might be able to help. Companies sometimes feel the government does not care about them anyway; there is a certain cynicism in that regard. But
Foreign Takeovers Review Act
here would be a real role for the department to play as the helpers of small industry in Canada.
You might, of course, get a situation where the only way to save the company would be to sell out to a foreign corporation, but on the other hand situations would be brought to the minister's attention of which formerly he and his officials had been unaware. This would enable them to go to the root cause of foreign takeovers in Canada. While legislation of itself might have some value, it does not solve the root problem. There are some things we do not understand about takeovers and about why we are so dominated by foreign ownership. We must deal with these questions, and legislation in itself is not sufficient answer.
This would be a wonderful opportunity for the minister to accept the amendment. His department would look at every takeover and would then be in a position to analyse the reason for the takeover and to consider offering assistance. Perhaps it is the sort of thing his department can do now. I am sure there are people who come to the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and are surprised at the amount of assistance available. In spite of publicity and what I think is general knowledge about services available, some small businessmen still have not a clue as to the kind of assistance available to them from the federal government and certain provincial governments.
The minister has talked about rationalization. Perhaps this is a way the minister can engage in a rationalization program. Instead of talking about it and making brilliant speeches, he could do something about this and provide opportunities for development and financing. He may say that his terms of reference are not as broad as he might wish; but if they are not, they should be. After all, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce was set up supposedly for the purpose of assisting business generally. If it cannot assist to the extent required, it should seek a broader mandate and greater responsibility.
These are a few of the things that I suggest would be of advantage. If this bill goes through without the kind of amendment proposed by the hon. member for Selkirk, it will in effect be useless. That is one of the reasons we urge acceptance of the amendment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my unhappy duty to bring before this House a bill to terminate the illegal work stoppages at the St. Lawrence ports of Montreal, Quebec City and Trois-Rivieres and to provide for the orderly resumption of operations at those ports. The government asks Parliament for this enactment because in its judgment the public and national interest require an end to this illegal situation and an end to the economic situation which is working severe hardship and damage not only on the three communites involved but on the country at large.
Acts of Parliament to terminate industrial disputes are infrequent. Indeed, it might not be going too far to say they are rare. There have been five acts over the past 30 years to bring an end to industrial disputes when the parties have failed to reach agreement in the normal process of collective bargaining. This bill, though, is exceptional for an additional reason. It does not terminate a collective bargaining dispute. It does not terminate that kind of dispute where a legal strike may be in progress. It does not terminate it in the sense that various differences between the two parties have been unable to be resolved.
Unlike previous acts of Parliament, this bill would terminate an unlawful situation, an unlawful strike which has been called after a three-year collective bargaining
July 5, 1972

agreement had been entered into in April of this year and at a time when a difference arose over the interpretation of clauses of that agreement. Subsequent to this basic source of dispute, that is to say, subsequent to the disagreement over what was the meaning of certain clauses and over what right the employer had to redeploy men in a certain fashion, there arose differences over the conditions of return to work under a contract which provided for a proper form of job security based on 37 guaranteed weeks of pay. This complex issue of return to work has become part of the difficulty in which we now find ourselves.
The debate in this House on Friday June 16 reviewed many of the basic issues in the current situation. However, I should like to place before the House now a factual account, a sequence of events which led up to this situation. On May 16 a work stoppage began. The basic issue which precipitated it was whether or not management had the right to break up longshoremen gangs prior to the introduction of the computer despatch system to be inaugurated approximately in mid-September. Management in Montreal took the initiative of breaking up work gangs and redeploying men not required to work a hatch to other work in a shed. The longshoremen's union contended management did not have this right until introduction of the computer despatch system, and the work stoppage began. I will come later to the question of the legality of the actions taken.
I immediately instructed our Montreal industrial specialist, Mr. Charles Poirier, to meet with the parties and urge that they refer this matter to arbitration as provided for in the collective agreement. Both sides declined to take that step. On May 15 I received a telegram from the MEA. If I may, I shall use the abbreviation MEA in referring to the Maritime Employers Association which is an association comprising some 51 stevedoring, shipping and other companies. The telegram requested I grant consent to prosecute the union for breach of contract. However, it was pointed out to the MEA that the appropriate remedy for the solution lay in the arbitration procedure of the collective agreement which provided that either party could initiate arbitration.
On May 30 the MEA announced that it had suspended the longshoremen. On June 5 I sent telegrams to both parties again urging that their differences be submitted to the procedure specified by law and asked them to advise me of their willingness to place their differences before the arbitrator named in the agreement. In a further exchange of telegrams in the next few days I continued to urge the parties to submit their dispute to arbitration. On June 19 I informed both parties that unless advised by return telegram that either party was ready to proceed to arbitration on the matter involved in violation of their collective agreement, it would be my intention to appoint an industrial inquiry commission to investigate the dispute, provided that the employers terminated the suspension of the longshoremen and provided that the longshoremen returned to work. I also indicated that I stood ready to meet the representatives of the parties in Ottawa at the earliest possible date to discuss such arrangements.
On June 20 and 21, together with my officials, I met with both parties in Ottawa to discuss the conditions which
St. Lawrence Ports Operations Bill
might be worked out for the lifting of the suspension and the return of the longshoremen to work. My position is, and has been, that there are four types of disputes dealt with in existing Canadian legislation governing the collective bargaining relationship:	First, disputes as to
representation of employees by a trade union. This is the normal dispute over union recognition. It is not the kind of dispute we are facing. Second, disputes as to the interpretation, application or violation of the provisions of a collective agreement. These are grievance disputes over rights. This is the kind of dispute we are facing. Third, disputes as to unfair labour practices. Fourth, disputes over the negotiation of conditions of employment to be included in a collective agreement. These are interest disputes.
The type of dispute with which we are concerned in this situation falls into the second one mentioned-disputes concerning the interpretation, application or violation of the provisions of a collective agreement. This type of dispute must, under existing legislation, be submitted to arbitration for final settlement which is binding on all parties and on all employees. The legislation requires that every collective agreement must contain a provision for the final settlement of disputes concerning its meaning or violation. Where such a provision is lacking, the Canada Labour Relations Board may prescribe a procedure for final settlement of grievance disputes. This is a distinctly Canadian procedure, dating from 1944.
The collective agreement between the International Longshoremen's Association and the Maritime Employers Association does set out the grievance procedure in article 5. I shall not read that procedure; we covered it fairly adequately in our debate on June 16. Subsequent to my meetings with the parties in Ottawa on June 22, the MEA advised me that it had decided to initiate arbitration and formally requested Judge Alan Gold, the first arbitrator named in the agreement, to arbitrate the issues in dispute. The union, however, refused to participate in the arbitration hearings which commenced on June 27. Union officers, with counsel, made an appearance at the arbitration hearings on Wednesday, June 28, only for the purpose of arguing that the issues in dispute were not arbitrable.
The arbitrator dealt with the four issues that had been submitted to him by the MEA and concluded as follows. I would like to read one or two pages which comprise the conclusions of the arbitrator since I think it would be valuable to all hon. members to have these in front of them. I quote from page 21 of the arbitrator's decision dated June 29 in Montreal.

(3)	That the strike by the union and its members is illegal, constituting work stoppages in violation of article 6 of the agreement and contrary to law;

quence were lawful and should have been obeyed by the employees concerned.
Montreal, June 29, 1972
Alan B. Gold, Arbitrator.
Following the release of the arbitrator's report, the ILA held a meeting and decided that they would not accept the arbitrator's award.
As I indicated earlier, I could not offer the parties mediation services until the provisions of the law and the provisions of the collective agreement in respect of arbitration had been utilized. However, once the arbitrator had made his report, the situation was such that I could proffer mediation on the issues impeding, the lifting of suspensions and the return to work.
On Friday, June 30, I directed the Deputy Minister, Mr. Bernard Wilson, and the Assistant Deputy Minister, Industrial Relations, Mr. W. P. Kelly, to proceed to Montreal with a view to arranging meetings between the MEA and the ILA and, if possible, to mediate conditions that would enable the ports to be re-opened.
The key issues involved in a return to work appeared to be the lifting of the suspension of the employees by the employers, agreement by the union and employees to accept the arbitrator's awards and return to work, the calling back to work of the employees as and when work became available, and the most important item which had to do with the job security provisions of the collective agreement. My officials conducted intensive mediation over the holiday weekend for some four days and when it was evident that the parties could not reach agreement, they submitted a detailed proposal recommending the conditions which should prevail to bring about lifting of the suspensions and a return to work. The recommendations were to be submitted to union meetings on July 4, yesterday, and the MEA was to consider the proposal the same day.
I have heard officially from the parties to the dispute in telegrams which I have here with me. I should indicate to the House that late last evening I received a telegram from the Maritime Employers Association which I will read in whole. It reads as follows:
The Maritime Employers Association accepts the proposal outlined in your return to work arrangement dated July 3, 1972 for the ports of Montreal, Quebec and Trois-Rivieres.
A. E. Masters President M.E.A.
I received official notice, although informal notice was available earlier, early this afternoon from Mr. Norman Quigley, international vice-president of the longshoremen's union and president of the local at Trois-Rivieres, and in his wire he speaks for the two locals situated at Trois-Rivieres and Quebec City. I will read his telegram. It, too, is short.
Dear Sir,
Memberships of local 1846 and 1739 have accepted proposals made by government representatives with one condition that any legal procedures will not be taken against any officers or members and union of above mentioned local.
July 5, 1972

The reference to legal procedures is to legal procedures initiated by various employers with respect to the illegal work stoppage. I have received a wire today from Mr. St. Onge, president of local 375 of Montreal. Perhaps I should read that in full, but it is rather lengthy.
Mr. Minister, following the recommendations made by your deputy minister on July 3, the International Longshoremen's Association, local 375, held a special general meeting of its membership in Montreal on July 4. While accepting the principle of returning to work as soon as possible, the members of the association have unanimously decided to reject the recommendation concerning the suspension of the job security plan until October 15, 1972 , a date which was deemed totally unacceptable. The members have set as a condition for returning to work that the job guarantee be restored approximately one week after the activities are resumed in the port of Montreal and that management give up the idea of any legal proceedings and action against the union and its officers. The officers of the association are available to meet you at any time in order to reach a satisfactory agreement whereby work can be resumed as soon as possible.
Those were the responses, Mr. Speaker. Work in fact is not being resumed at the ports and in the circumstances I have to assume that the proposals of mediation have not been successful in bringing about a termination of the dispute and that the proposals have in fact been rejected. May I now come to the principles in this bill.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE PORTS OPERATIONS BILL MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION OF LONGSHORING AND RELATED OPERATIONS
speechtext: Would the minister permit a question? Was part of the agreement that the court action that was contemplated was left in abeyance? Was this part of the recommendation?

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE PORTS OPERATIONS BILL MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION OF LONGSHORING AND RELATED OPERATIONS
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker; the question of court action was no part of the proposals put forward by the mediators. If the House would like me to read the proposals, I will do so. It might take me a moment to locate them.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE PORTS OPERATIONS BILL MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION OF LONGSHORING AND RELATED OPERATIONS
speechtext: The question I was really asking is this: Is this a new factor in the negotiations that your deputy minister had undertaken? Has this been added since, or was it part of the negotiations in which he had been involved and in the proposition that he put forward to the parties on June 3?

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE PORTS OPERATIONS BILL MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION OF LONGSHORING AND RELATED OPERATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will check into that to be absolutely precise, but my preliminary answer is that the question of legal action did not enter into the main negotiations, that the proposals had been worked out prior to that issue arising, that Mr. St. Onge raised it at the last moment as he was leaving. But I will check into these factors. I would like to report again, to be absolutely precise on this point.
The bill before us, if enacted by Parliament, expresses the will of this Parliament that the ports be reopened. It expresses the national interest, that the public interest lies in the opening of these ports. The object of the bill, as hon. members will see, is to achieve the resumption of long-shoring and related operations in the three ports of Montreal, Quebec City and Trois-Rivieres. In the bill we notice the requirement that each employer must resume long-shoring and related operations in the ports of Montreal, Quebec City and Trois-Rivieres immediately after the bill comes into force. That is set forth in clause 3. Second, each union officer must give notice to the members of the union that any strike declaration, authorization or direction previously given is invalid. That is in clause 4. Each
St. Lawrence Ports Operations Bill
union officer must comply with any order or request for the dispatch of longshoremen. Again that is in clause 4.
Every longshoreman coming under the collective agreement must, when so required, return to the duties of his employment. That is laid out in clause 5. Again, according to clause 5 union officials shall not impede or prevent, or attempt to impede or prevent the longshoremen from returning to work. Clause 6 provides that a further strike or lockout is prohibited under the terms of the collective agreement. This clause in substance repeats a section of the Canada Labour Code, section 128, except that it also forbids a union officer from declaring or otherwise authorizing a strike which is not provided for in the legislation already in force.
Clause 7 relates to the job security plan, which is a major impediment to returning to work. Clause 7 suspends the provisions relating to the job security plan in the collective agreement until such date as an arbitrator may specify for the resumption of operation of the plan. Under clause 7(2) an arbitrator may fix the date on which the plan will come into effect and may make such modifications to the plan as are required to give effect to it. That is an important part of the bill in front of us, Mr. Speaker. I trust all hon. members are aware of the job security plan. It is that very particular plan in this collective agreement which provides 37 guaranteed weeks of pay to the longshoremen whether in fact they are working or not. The difficulty would immediately be apparent to hon. members that if men report for work but there is no work to be done, the employer is not in a position to live up to the guarantee written into the agreement.
Again, clause 7 suspends those provisions until an arbitrator, considering all of the factors, specifies a date for the operation of the plan, and necessarily in that event the original plan becomes modified and he is given the power under this bill to make such modifications to the plan as are required to give effect to it on the date selected.
Clause 8 provides that the minister may in the future refer a matter in dispute to arbitration if the parties do not do so within a reasonable time. The final clause provides for the coming into force of the bill on the day following its being assented to, and that it expires with the collective agreement on December 31, 1974, unless earlier by proclamation.
I think those are the main facts of the situation, Mr. Speaker. The main reason for coming to Parliament at this time is to ask it to do what it is asked very infrequently to do in the federal jurisdiction but must be asked to do when facilities of such national importance as these three St. Lawrence docks have been closed going into the eighth week in circumstances which give us no assurance that they will be reopened in the near future, and when the public interest has been clearly engaged to the extent that it has. I would, therefore, ask Parliament to support the government in this bill.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE PORTS OPERATIONS BILL MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION OF LONGSHORING AND RELATED OPERATIONS
speechtext: Secondly, this House is not in possession of the economic facts and the financial factors involved. maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE PORTS OPERATIONS BILL MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION OF LONGSHORING AND RELATED OPERATIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE PORTS OPERATIONS BILL MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION OF LONGSHORING AND RELATED OPERATIONS
speechtext: I should like to put this question to the minister. Why did he not put any clauses containing sanctions in the bill? Would he tell the House what range of sanctions he feels the government has available to it if the provisions of the bill are not followed?

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE PORTS OPERATIONS BILL MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION OF LONGSHORING AND RELATED OPERATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the first part of that question, I would answer this way. This bill is based on the presumption that when Parliament has clearly expressed its will, and has represented the public interest to the parties in this dispute, they will conform to the specific and express will of Parliament. Second, this is based on the constructive approach to the relationships between the two parties to bring about not only an early resumption of work but constructive relationships for the future. It is not that there are no sanctions behind a bill of this kind.
In answer to the second part of the question, let me quote from section 115 of the Criminal Code of Canada which relates to the disobedience of a statute of this Parliament:
Everyone who, without lawful excuse, contravenes an act of the Parliament of Canada by wilfully doing anything that it forbids or by wilfully omitting to do anything that it requires to be done is, unless some penalty or punishment is expressly provided by law, guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for two years.
Other provisions of the Code, Mr. Speaker, particularly section 646, provide that fines may be imposed in lieu of imprisonment. I think that answers the question.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE PORTS OPERATIONS BILL MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION OF LONGSHORING AND RELATED OPERATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can understand that the minister and the government did not want to become involved with the collective bargaining process because, after all, this process is supposed to settle everything. The minister did not want to intervene because, as he said, if he did that would be the end of the collective bargaining process. What disturbs me, Mr. Speaker, is that a pattern has been set. We have seen a collective agreement ignored, we have seen the Minister of Labour (Mr. O'Connell's) directives ignored, we have seen the Quebec Superior Court ignored and we have seen Mr. Justice Gold's arbitration award ignored. Mr. Speaker, the third party involved, the general public was ignored; the national interest was ignored.
All I can say is that this strike has been disastrous, has been catastrophic, in its effects. Surely, one does not have to go into great detail in order to point out that it has inflicted severe economic loss. I say, Mr. Speaker, that it has inflicted inconvenience upon the nation. I say, Mr. Speaker, that it has created unemployment, that all these

July 5, 1972

losses are damaging to the economy and well-being of this country. They are irreparable, Mr. Speaker.
I understand that some 100 ships have been turned away from the ports of Montreal, Trois-Rivieres and Quebec. I understand shipping agents have announced their intention to seek other ports through which they can discharge their goods. What does this mean? It means that the entire St. Lawrence Seaway and the port of Montreal have been drastically affected, and as a result that this nation has been drastically affected.
Let us consider some figures relating to the port of Montreal. All cargoes handled at National Harbours Board ports in Canada during 1971 totalled a record of 93.7 million tons, up 7.9 per cent from 1970. The port of Montreal, however, shows a decline of 5.4 per cent, to 23-odd million tons, in the same period. And what has the strike done? Has it alleviated that situation? No, it has aggravated it.
To be honest, I must concede that as a result of what has happened in Montreal the Atlantic provinces have profited. I am sure that the port of Hamilton has profited. However, I am not here to speak about any profit that may come to some as a result of hardship that may be endured in any other area of the country. In the long run we shall all be worse off. What I am speaking about is the public interest of the entire country to which I belong.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE PORTS OPERATIONS BILL MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION OF LONGSHORING AND RELATED OPERATIONS

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE PORTS OPERATIONS BILL MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION OF LONGSHORING AND RELATED OPERATIONS
speechtext: That is why I do not hesitate to stand up and speak on this bill. For some reason or other it suddenly awoke to the fact that the most important party in those negotiations was not management nor labour but was the consumer, the Canadian people. It suddenly realized that the public interest must prevail. We on this side of the House have said that constantly. We have said that the public interest must prevail, if necessary to the detriment of the two parties involved in the dispute.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE PORTS OPERATIONS BILL MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION OF LONGSHORING AND RELATED OPERATIONS
speechtext:
I do not know whether clause 7 is acceptable. I want to know why the proposals of the Deputy Minister of Labour, a man with unquestioned expertise in labour matters, were not accepted. Of course, this has already been explained. After four days of negotiation he came forward with certain proposals. Mr. Speaker, the deputy minister knows in which direction we ought to move. He came forward with certain proposals, but this bill does not incorporate them.
I heard the minister say he did not want Parliament to intervene in matters which should be left to the collective bargaining process. Don't give me that nonsense! The government brought in Bill C-183 by which it permitted agreements to be altered if technological change was involved. The government acted effectively in that regard and thought nothing of it. Why? It acted in that field because that was not as contentious an issue as the one we are now considering. The government stayed clear of this issue. It ignored the recommendations of one of the best men that it has in the entire department. Its excuse for not including them is weak and unacceptable.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE PORTS OPERATIONS BILL MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION OF LONGSHORING AND RELATED OPERATIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE PORTS OPERATIONS BILL MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION OF LONGSHORING AND RELATED OPERATIONS
speechtext:
Let me read what the deputy minister brought forward:
1.	The union accepts the arbitration award of June 29, subject to any rights of appeal that it may wish to exercise.
2.	The suspension of all of the employees, including permanent employees, will be lifted immediately and they will be called back to work as and when work becomes available.
3.	The job security provisions in the collective agreements will not be given effect from the date of return to work until midnight on October 15, 1972. The job security provisions will apply in full during the remainder of 1972 and during 1973 and 1974 as set out in the collective agreements.
4.	Vacation pay due under the collective agreements will be paid to the employees as soon as it is possible to have staff available to issue the cheques.
Again, I want to know why the suggestions of a man of great calibre, a man who was given all available assistance by the Department of Labour and who sat in consultation with management and with the longshoremen's union, were ignored. Why did the minister leave his proposals out? Surely the deputy minister had good reason for putting them forward.
Consider the matter of job security which would involve, I think, for each man 35 weeks at about $188 a week. That comes to a lot of money. If these men go back to work, and if the job security part of the agreement is to operate immediately, where is the money to come from? You must remember that in the collective agreement provisions were made not only for that matter but also for a pension scheme that was admirable. So if some sort of time lag is not introduced here, somebody will be in trouble. I expect that the arbitrator who will be involved in this matter will be cognizant of that particular set of circumstances. I do not know why they are not spelled out in the bill. The minister tried to explain this matter.
Let me run over some other matters. Other spokesmen will speak on this. I am pleased to see that the government House leader, after having been enlightened by members of the opposition, agreed that this matter should be considered in committee of the whole. Why not? I know that

there is the question of calling witnesses, but surely we know what the situation is all about. The papers have been full of it for the past seven weeks. We have a fair idea. The idea is to get people back to work, not to hear the same arguments over again.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext: The idea is to let those who wish to condemn the government because of their ineptitude stand up and talk about it. On the other hand, I know that the government likes to play games. They have the foreign takeovers bill and the FISP program.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE PORTS OPERATIONS BILL MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION OF LONGSHORING AND RELATED OPERATIONS

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE PORTS OPERATIONS BILL MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION OF LONGSHORING AND RELATED OPERATIONS
speechtext:
I hear the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin). He must feel like a lost soul, along with the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro). They cannot seem to get anywhere. If they had presented proper bills, those bills would have been passed forthwith. We cannot let that kind of nonsense go to the people.
The disheartening thing about this situation is that after three years of work, we have to intervene. After three years of work by many people, federal department mediators, union representatives and employers as well as a number of committees, an historic document was prepared. I see the former Minister of Labour, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Mackasey), smiling. With all respect to the present Minister of Labour (Mr. O'Connell), it was through the efforts of the former Minister of Labour that attempts were made to resolve these situations prior to them confronting the country. A significant agreement was ratified on March 29, 1970 by the Maritime Employers Association and the International Longshoremans Association, local 371, affecting 3,200 longshoremen. The terms were important. The unions agreed to give up featherbedding. This was the most important thing.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE PORTS OPERATIONS BILL MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION OF LONGSHORING AND RELATED OPERATIONS
speechtext:
If you do not know what it is all about, read the collective agreement. Management agreed to meet some of the union's most serious claims. Management agreed to ironclad job security and a vastly improved pension plan. Why the strike? This was supposed to be the classic document which would help put the collective bargaining process on the road. What happened? I do not want to be repetitious. We know what happened. Why the strike? As I understand it, and I can be checked if I am wrong, it was based on the contention that the employers tried to break up the 16 member gang system before the computer could do it properly in September. Does that really make sense? This is how the whole thing started.
Let me tell you what the collective agreement states. I remember the Minister of Labour saying that they must go to arbitration if they have a grievance. The document to which I am referring is approximately one half inch thick. It covers everything you could mention. It provides for a grievance procedure. I may be paraphrasing, but it

states that if you have a grievance you have to follow the arbitration proceedings that were determined after three years of blood, sweat and tears. The agreement reads:
A request for arbitration may be initiated by either the union or the Maritime Employers Association. The party requesting the arbitration shall set forth in writing the matter submitted to the arbitrator and send a copy of it to the other party.
I do not know what happened to that provision. It sounds simple. As a matter of fact, after three years of work, we had a very simple solution; submit your grievances to arbitration. This is how we were going to solve our problem.
There is another matter to which the minister did not refer. Possibly he did not have time. My time is running out also. The agreement reads:
Pending disposal of a dispute in accordance with the arbitration procedure,-
This is spelled out on a page and a half.
-men will work as instructed by the companies subject to the provisions contained dealing with help and safety.
I did not make that up. It is in the agreement that was signed by the two respective parties. I could be repetitious and say, as someone else has said, the agreement does not count. The procedure is set out right there. There is one clause in the agreement that should be put on the record because it reveals the hypocrisy of the situation that existed until the government had the intestinal fortitude to bring in this bill. I may be quoting out of context, but it reads:
In view of the orderly arrangements provided by this agreement for the settling of grievances, the union agrees with the companies that during the lifetime of this agreement-
Incidentally, it is a three year agreement.
-there shall be no strikes, slowdowns or stoppages of work, either complete or partial, and the companies agree there will be no lock-out.
Did you know that was in the agreement? What is the collective agreement worth? I did not know it was in the agreement until I saw it three or four days ago.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE PORTS OPERATIONS BILL MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION OF LONGSHORING AND RELATED OPERATIONS
speechtext: It may be. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, why do the parties not abide by that provision after the three years of blood, sweat and tears it took to arrive at an agreement? It is all right for the leader of the New Democratic Party to say that this clause is in all the agreements, but this is pretty important. It was not drafted overnight by two 15 cent lawyers.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE PORTS OPERATIONS BILL MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION OF LONGSHORING AND RELATED OPERATIONS
speechtext: Who are they?

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE PORTS OPERATIONS BILL MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION OF LONGSHORING AND RELATED OPERATIONS
speechtext:
There are a few. Others will likely want to speak on this bill. As I have already said, we are not going to prolong this matter. However, certain positions, facts and problems have not been explored. They should not only be placed before this government and the members of this House, but the people of Canada.
St. Lawrence Ports Operations Bill
In closing, I wish to refer to a speech that I was going to give somewhere at some time. It is extremely appropriate at this time.
Many Canadians believe that labour-management relations, whether in the public or private sector, appear to be more concerned about and involved with confrontation rather than negotiation, thereby leaving a lot to be desired in the area of collective bargaining. The whole collective bargaining system is presently under serious attack and question and one is constantly reminded of its imperfections. This case is a classic one when we cite the agreement that was signed in March of 1972. In particular, the strike which is an integral and hard won part of the process, has not escaped serious questioning.
It takes only one or two strikes or the threat of them, particularly in areas where it appears the public interest in terms of health, safety and general well-being of the individual is, or could be, adversely affected, to raise cries about the failure of the collective bargaining system, the need for some alternatives and the need for legislation banning strikes. This growing attitude towards strikes stems in part from the fact that more people who are not involved in union or management, and even some within that area, now realize that strikes are neither against the government nor the private employer, but against them, the ultimate consumers, the vast majority of whom have not been represented at the bargaining table.
That is the point we have to be concerned about today. That is the point I want to emphasize. We must move in the direction of being cognizant of the third party who is not represented at the bargaining table. More Canadians are becoming increasingly alarmed about the disruptive nature of the strike and point to the seaway strike in 1968, the postal strikes of 1968, 1970 and 1972, the strikes of the air traffic controllers as well as electronic technicians, CBC technicians and now the longshoremen. All of these, as I have said, have inflicted economic loss on the nation and created unemployment, thereby giving Canadians reason to demand from the government action for the protection of the public interest and that it carry out its public responsibility. This demand, to me, in view of all the circumstances, is not unreasonable nor unwarranted because the public interest must prevail.
As I have said, Mr. Speaker, we will be pleased to discuss the bill further. We have not really had an opportunity to digest it, but by the time it gets through committee of the whole I am sure it will be a bill that has been given proper consideration in the time allowed. I anxiously await its early second reading and passage so we can get the economy moving again and open the ports of Montreal, Quebec and Trois-Rivieres.
